analysis.one_liner: Declares a national housing emergency and uses wartime production powers to boost homebuilding.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 8, 2026 with zero cosponsors and referred to two House committees; no hearing, markup, or vote has occurred, and Congress adjourns in January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the President declare housing a national emergency and invoke the Defense Production Act — a wartime law normally used to force priority production of critical materials — to expand U.S. home construction. It would suspend several federal rules during the emergency, including some environmental reviews for HUD-funded housing, set a national minimum building code, and condition federal transportation and block grants on cities and states permitting more housing. It would also bar local governments from enforcing land-use rules that substantially burden housing construction, and the emergency would end when 4 million additional units are built or on October 1, 2031, whichever comes first. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and priced-out first-time buyers, whom the bill's own findings describe as facing a shortage of at least 4 million units and record-low first-time buying, would gain if the additional supply actually gets built and lowers prices. Homebuilders and developers would also gain from faster permitting, a lighter federal rulebook, and Defense Production Act support for materials. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: The bill finds that roughly 75% of U.S. households cannot afford a median-priced home and projects the housing deficit growing to nearly 10 million units by 2035, and aims its supply push at that gap. [S2]
It would let the President use Defense Production Act authorities to increase domestic production of construction materials and prioritize housing alongside energy as a critical domestic need. [S2]

It would tie federal transportation and block grant money to local zoning reforms — smaller lots, duplexes and fourplexes in single-family zones, accessory dwelling units, faster permitting — that independent housing research links to lower rents and prices. [S2]
Its findings claim closing the shortfall would unlock nearly 2 million jobs, including over 700,000 construction jobs, and add nearly $2 trillion to GDP through 2035. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Local governments would lose significant control over zoning while the emergency lasts, and communities near HUD-funded projects would lose ordinary environmental review. Taxpayers would bear the cost of whatever incentives the President orders under the Defense Production Act. Some residents of deregulated neighborhoods could see more construction nearby with fewer of the review processes that previously gave them a say. [S2]

drawbacks.text: During the emergency, HUD-funded housing preservation and infill projects would skip federal environmental review entirely, and multi-program projects would get only one combined review — trading environmental and community protections for speed. [S2]

The bill would outright prohibit any state or local land-use rule that imposes a 'substantial burden' on housing construction, a broad federal preemption of zoning that takes power away from the governments closest to residents. [S2]

It sets the national minimum code at the 2009 International Residential Code — roughly 15 years older than the current edition — which builders' critics could read as a floor that permits cheaper, less energy-efficient construction. [S2]

It suspends several affordable-housing program rules under the Cranston-Gonzalez Act and lets a HUD Secretary's Buy America waiver be deemed issued after 30 days if not reviewed, loosening guardrails in the name of speed. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — build far more housing because scarcity is driving prices up — addresses a real and well-documented problem, and the grant condition uses a lever with evidence behind it. But the bill buys speed by stripping environmental review, preempting local zoning outright, and freezing the building code at a 2009 standard, and it relies on the President actually invoking emergency authorities the bill can only request. It is a broad deregulatory experiment, not a targeted affordability program, and it never came close to being tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on September 8, 2026 and referred to the Financial Services and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote. [S4]

narrative.text: Rep. Chrissy Houlahan introduced the National Housing Emergency Act of 2026 on September 8, 2026. [S1]
It was referred to the Committee on Financial Services and, in addition, to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure for the provisions within their jurisdiction. [S4]
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor. [S3]
Beyond the referral, the bill has taken no further action: no committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or companion Senate bill appears in the record. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With Congress set to end on January 3, 2027 and the bill only weeks old, the practical outcome so far is that the status quo holds: local zoning authority, existing environmental review requirements, and current building codes all stay in place, which is the position local governments and community-review processes prefer. Homebuilders and buyers remain where they were, since the emergency and supply push never started. [S4]

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo and its defenders

for.name: Rep. Chrissy Houlahan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case, in its findings, that a 4-million-unit shortage justifies an emergency declaration and a supply push. [S1] [S2]

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken, and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknown. [S3]

industries.note: The bill would clear away permitting delays, some environmental reviews, and grant conditions that slow builders down, and its findings credit overregulation with about 25% of the cost of a new home. Cheaper, faster construction largely aligns with buyer interests, but shedding environmental review and pre-2009 code standards raises builders' margins in ways buyers do not share.

Adding residential construction to the Defense Production Act would let the President give housing materials priority status and incentives, expanding demand and production for domestic manufacturers alongside the public goal of more supply.

Federal block grant and highway money would be conditioned on permitting more housing, and during the emergency no local land-use rule could substantially burden residential construction. Governments closest to residents would lose the zoning control they have historically defended.

The bill would let manufactured homes be placed in areas zoned for single-family houses and sets the HUD manufactured-housing code as an accepted standard, opening a large new market for factory-built housing.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors, no committee action, and roughly four months left in the Congress, the bill will almost certainly expire in committee at the end of this session without a hearing or a vote.
